topic: The political fight dominating July 23-24, 2026 is President Trump's new global tariff — imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 on the ground that 60 trading partners have failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Ambassador Jamieson Greer took final action on July 23; the duties took effect on July 24, the exact day the administration's temporary Section 122 'balance of payments' surcharge hit its statutory 150-day expiration. The new rates are 10 percent for 17 economies that have adopted or committed to forced-labor import prohibitions (including Canada, Mexico, India and the UK), 12.5 percent for 38 others (including China and Vietnam), and 10-12.5 percent net of MFN duties for the EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan — covering economies that account for roughly 99.4 percent of U.S. imports, with carve-outs for energy, fertilizer, some food, USMCA-qualifying goods, pharmaceuticals and articles already under Section 232. The checkable core: whether Section 301 — a statute whose enumerated forced-labor clause targets a country that 'permits any form of forced or compulsory labor,' not one that fails to police its own imports — can carry an economy-wide tariff on nearly every U.S. trading partner five months after the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that the emergency-powers statute could not. Within hours two small importers, represented by the conservative-libertarian Liberty Justice Center, sued in the Court of International Trade calling the forced-labor rationale a pretext to recreate the tariffs the Court struck down. Steel and machinist unions praised the action; Rep. Richard Neal called the justification 'too convenient to be taken seriously.'
question: On July 23-24, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative concluded 60 parallel Section 301 investigations and imposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on nearly every significant U.S. trading partner, finding that each economy's failure to impose or effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods made with forced labor is 'unreasonable' and burdens U.S. commerce. The administration and its supporters answer that forced labor is a real and enormous problem — the ILO counts 27.6 million people in forced labour — that the United States has banned forced-labor imports since 1930 while its partners largely have not, that Section 301 expressly names forced labor among 'unreasonable' practices, that USTR ran the full statutory process (60 investigations opened March 12, findings June 2, 1,600-plus written comments, 100-plus witnesses across two rounds of hearings), and that the seven economies which strengthened their laws had their rates cut from 12.5 to 10 percent — proof the tariff is a lever, not a pretext. Critics — congressional Democrats, importers, trading partners, trade lawyers, and free-market conservatives — answer that the action landed on the precise day the Section 122 stopgap expired, replaces a 10 percent global tariff with a 10-12.5 percent global tariff covering 99.4 percent of imports, applies economy-wide rather than to forced-labor goods, and follows a February Supreme Court ruling that the president cannot tax imports without clear congressional authorization; the Treasury Secretary's own post-ruling plan, they note, was to bridge with Section 122 while Sections 232 and 301 processes concluded so revenue would be roughly unchanged. Which side's checkable claims hold up?
summary:
The most-argued domestic policy story of July 24, 2026 is the new Section 301 'forced labor' tariff — the fourth statute in five months through which the administration has reached substantially the same global tariff after the Supreme Court struck down the first. PBS NewsHour led its Friday broadcast with it; the trade bar, congressional Democrats, foreign governments and a conservative-libertarian litigation shop all reacted the same day. The day leans modestly toward the critics on the checkable merits — not because forced labor is a fake problem, and not because Section 301 is obviously unavailable, but because the administration's strongest factual assertions are overstated while the critics' load-bearing claims sit on statutes, dockets and the government's own record.

What is verified and not seriously disputed: the White House memorandum of July 23 and USTR's release impose 10 percent on 17 economies, 12.5 percent on 38 others, and 10-12.5 percent net of MFN on five more, across 60 economies representing about 99.4 percent of U.S. imports. The Section 122 surcharge it replaced took effect February 24, 2026 and hit its statutory 150-day ceiling — 'a period not exceeding 150 days (unless such period is extended by Act of Congress)' — on July 24, the same day. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026) the Court held 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, with the Chief Justice invoking the requirement of clear congressional authorization. The Congressional Research Service, three days before the action, flagged exactly the questions now in litigation: whether a failure to police imports is an actionable 'act, policy, or practice'; whether tariffs on economies covering 'more than 99% of U.S. imports' invite major-questions scrutiny; and whether the administrative record supports the rates chosen. Section 301's enumerated forced-labor clause reaches a country whose conduct 'permits any form of forced or compulsory labor' — its own labor practices — though the statutory list is expressly non-exhaustive.

The administration holds real ground the honest version must credit. The forced-labor problem is real and large. Section 301 is a genuine, long-used congressional delegation of tariff authority — the Court did not touch it in February, and a Democratic administration used it in May 2024 to raise Chinese EV duties from 25 to 100 percent. USTR ran a real process, not a press release: 60 investigations opened March 12, findings June 2, over 1,600 written comments, more than 100 witnesses at the July 7-9 hearings. Rates were differentiated by conduct, and seven economies that adopted or committed to prohibitions moved from 12.5 to 10 percent — which is what a lever looks like rather than a flat tax. The Steelworkers and the Machinists, unions that rarely praise this president, endorsed the action.

What pushes the needle is that the two claims doing the most work are checkably overstated. Ambassador Greer said the United States 'has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it' — the ban does date to the Tariff Act of 1930, but its 'consumptive demand' exception, which exempted goods not produced domestically in sufficient quantity, was not repealed until February 24, 2016. And the remedy does not match the finding: the tariffs apply economy-wide rather than to forced-labor goods, and the rate schedule tracks whether a country has an import-ban statute more than any measured quantum of forced-labor trade. Add the timing to the day, and Michael Froman's contemporaneous description of the announced strategy — Section 122 as a 150-day bridge 'to launch and complete processes under other authorities, such as Sections 201, 232, 301, or 338' — and the pretext inference is not a smear; it is the administration's own published sequence. What the meter cannot decide: whether tariffs are a good instrument for human-rights enforcement, whether the cost to American consumers is worth the leverage, whether Congress should reclaim the tariff power it delegated, and whether a policy can be lawful when its author's motives are mixed.
verdict: On the checkable present-tense facts this leans toward the critics of the new Section 301 tariffs, modestly rather than decisively — the central legal question is genuinely unresolved, and no court had ruled as of July 24. Confirmed: the tariffs cover 60 economies and roughly 99.4 percent of U.S. imports at 10 to 12.5 percent; they took effect the same day the Section 122 surcharge hit its statutory 150-day limit, a limit that reads 'not exceeding 150 days (unless such period is extended by Act of Congress)'; the Supreme Court held on February 20 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; and the Congressional Research Service, on July 21, had already flagged the actionability, major-questions and administrative-record problems now pleaded in the Court of International Trade. Two of the administration's load-bearing assertions are overstated on the record: Ambassador Greer's 'nearly a century' of rigorous U.S. enforcement elides that the statute's consumptive-demand exception survived until February 2016, and the economy-wide remedy is broader than the practice found, which is the gap Section 301 case law has historically policed. The administration's real ground keeps this close: forced labor is a documented global problem, Section 301 is an explicit congressional delegation the February ruling left untouched and that a Democratic administration used in May 2024 to quadruple Chinese EV duties, USTR ran a full statutory process with 1,600-plus comments and 100-plus witnesses, seven economies earned rate cuts by changing their laws, and two major unions endorsed the action. The critics have their own overreach — the Court did not hold that all delegated tariff authority is void, and the party now calling unilateral Section 301 tariffs lawless built and expanded them two years ago. What the meter does not decide: whether tariffs are the right tool against forced labor, whether the consumer cost is worth the leverage, whether Congress should take its tariff power back, or whether mixed motives can invalidate an otherwise lawful action.

The controlling statutes were read at Cornell's U.S. Code: 19 U.S.C. 2411(d)(3)(B) for the enumerated 'unreasonable' practices including clause (iii)(III) on forced labor, 19 U.S.C. 2132 for the Section 122 15-percent/150-day limits, and 19 U.S.C. 1307 for the 1930 import ban and the February 24, 2016 repeal of the consumptive-demand exception. The Congressional Research Service Legal Sidebar LSB11460 (July 21, 2026) was read via EveryCRSReport because congress.gov returned HTTP 403; it is the source for the actionability, major-questions and record-support analysis. The Liberty Justice Center's press release (read directly) supplies the July 24 filing, the plaintiffs and counsel quotes; InsideTrade's report is paywalled and was used only to confirm the 'pretext' characterization visible above the wall. Neal's quote and foreign-government reactions; the trade-law firm analyses from Troutman Pepper Locke (read directly) for the effective-date mechanics, exemptions, TRQs and severability clause; Simon Lester's IELP blog (read directly) for the expert pretext-versus-lever debate; PBS NewsHour's July 24 rundown (read directly) confirming the tariffs led the day alongside the Iran war. One conflict is surfaced rather than smoothed: multiple trade-law firms date the tariffs' effect to 12:01 a.m. ET July 24, while Fox Business and Fortune described them as taking effect as the Section 122 duties expired 'Friday' — July 24, 2026 was itself a Friday, and the one-day discrepancy in some accounts is noted rather than resolved. left.label: Five months ago the Supreme Court told this president he cannot tax the country by decree. He responded by taxing it under a different number. On February 24 it was Section 122 — a balance-of-payments surcharge Congress capped at 15 percent and 150 days precisely so no president could make it permanent. On July 24, the day that clock ran out to the hour, the same global tariff reappeared wearing a human-rights costume: 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies covering 99.4 percent of everything America imports, justified by the discovery that our trading partners' import-enforcement statutes are not as good as ours. Notice what the remedy does not do. It does not tax forced-labor goods. It taxes coffee, watches, machine parts, everything, from countries whose sin is a paperwork gap — and it taxes them at a rate that has nothing to do with how much forced labor anyone measured. The Treasury Secretary's own plan, published in February, was to use Section 122 as a bridge until the 232 and 301 processes could restore the revenue. That is not a human-rights policy that happens to raise money; it is a revenue policy that happens to mention human rights. Americans will pay it at the register, and the courts will have to say, again, that Congress holds the taxing power.
left.framing: The critics' load-bearing claims are documentary and they hold: the Section 122 expiration date, the 99.4-percent coverage, the economy-wide rather than product-specific remedy, the Supreme Court's February holding, the Congressional Research Service's pre-action list of vulnerabilities, and the administration's own February description of the statute-substitution sequence. The strongest form of this case concedes what the meter credits to the other side — that forced labor is real and large, that Section 301 is a legitimate delegation the February ruling left intact, that USTR ran an actual notice-and-comment process with 1,600-plus comments and two rounds of hearings, that seven countries earned lower rates by changing their laws, and that two major unions endorsed the action. Where the case weakens is when critics slide from 'the Court struck IEEPA' to 'the Court already held this unlawful,' which is not what happened, and when Democrats who defended a 100-percent unilateral Section 301 tariff on Chinese EVs in May 2024 present unilateral Section 301 tariffs as inherently lawless now.
left.strongestPoint: The mismatch between the finding and the remedy is visible in the government's own documents, and it is the specific thing Section 301 review polices. USTR found that each economy failed to prohibit or enforce against imports of forced-labor goods; the tariff it imposed falls on all goods from those economies, at rates that track whether a country has an import-ban statute rather than any measured volume of forced-labor trade. Troutman Pepper Locke's analysis states it plainly: the duties apply 'economy-wide rather than only to forced-labor goods.' The Congressional Research Service, writing on July 21 before the action, had already framed the exposure — tariffs reaching economies that account for 'more than 99% of U.S. imports' invite the argument that this is an 'unheralded' and 'transformational' use of the statute requiring 'clear congressional authorization,' the same doctrine that killed the IEEPA tariffs in February. And the timing is not circumstantial atmosphere; it is a statutory fact: Section 122 permits a surcharge 'for a period not exceeding 150 days (unless such period is extended by Act of Congress),' the surcharge took effect February 24, and the replacement took effect the day it expired.
left.weakestPoint: The camp overstates what the Supreme Court decided and understates its own record. Learning Resources held that IEEPA — a statute that never mentions tariffs — does not authorize them; it did not hold that Congress's explicit tariff delegations are suspect, and Section 301 is about as explicit as delegations get. Two years ago a Democratic administration used the same statute, after the same kind of USTR review, to raise duties on Chinese electric vehicles from 25 to 100 percent and on solar cells from 25 to 50 percent, and congressional Democrats cheered; 'the executive cannot set tariffs unilaterally' is not a principle that survives contact with that record. The pretext charge, while well supported circumstantially, is a claim about motive, and mixed motives do not by themselves void an action that satisfies the statute. And the reflex to treat the forced-labor rationale as simply invented sits awkwardly beside the Steelworkers' and Machinists' endorsements and beside the seven rate reductions granted to countries that changed their laws.
left.unknowns: Whether the Court of International Trade will accept the pretext theory, apply major-questions scrutiny, or defer to USTR's record under ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious review is entirely open — the complaint was filed the same day the tariffs took effect. How much of the 99.4-percent import coverage is actually taxed after the energy, fertilizer, food, USMCA and Section 232 carve-outs is not established in any document read. Whether any of the 60 economies will in fact tighten enforcement in response, and whether USTR would then lower rates, cannot be known from the present record; Section 301 contains no formal adjustment mechanism.

right.label: Twenty-seven million people are in forced labour worldwide, and the United States is nearly alone in refusing to buy what they make. We banned convict and forced-labor imports in 1930. Our trading partners, ninety-six years later, mostly have not — fifty-four of the sixty largest have no such prohibition at all, and six more have one they do not enforce. That is not a technicality; it is a subsidy. Goods made by coerced workers flow through their supply chains, their producers get the cost advantage, and American steelworkers, shrimpers and manufacturers compete against it every day. Congress wrote Section 301 for exactly this: foreign practices that are unreasonable and burden American commerce, with forced labor named in the statute itself. So USTR did the work — sixty investigations opened in March, findings in June, sixteen hundred written comments, more than a hundred witnesses across two rounds of hearings — and set rates that move with conduct: seven countries that adopted or committed to prohibitions were cut from 12.5 to 10 percent. Energy, fertilizer, food, USMCA goods and steel are carved out. The Steelworkers and the Machinists back it. Decades of moral suasion did not eradicate forced labor from global supply chains. Market access might.
right.framing: The defenders' checkable strengths are genuine: forced labor is real and enormous, Section 301 is a valid and frequently used congressional delegation untouched by the February ruling, the statutory process was real rather than pro forma, the rate schedule is conduct-responsive, the carve-outs are substantial, and organized labor — not a natural ally — signed on. Where the case strains is in two places the record can test. First, Ambassador Greer's claim that the United States 'has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it' compresses a history in which the consumptive-demand exception hollowed out that ban until it was repealed in February 2016. Second, and more seriously for the litigation, the remedy is not tailored to the practice found: an economy-wide tariff on nearly every U.S. trading partner, landing the day a 150-day statutory clock expired, on a schedule the administration itself sketched in February as a way to keep tariff revenue roughly unchanged, is difficult to characterize as the narrowly appropriate response Section 301 contemplates. The argument that the tariff is a lever would be far stronger if the lever pulled only on forced-labor goods.
right.strongestPoint: The legal and procedural foundation is much sturdier than the 'obviously lawless' framing allows, and the process was real. Section 301 is an express congressional delegation of tariff authority whose text names forced or compulsory labor among 'unreasonable' practices and whose enumerated list is prefaced 'include, but are not limited to' — so the argument that a failure to police forced-labor imports falls outside the statute is a serious argument, not a slam dunk. The Supreme Court's February ruling turned on IEEPA's silence about tariffs; it says nothing about a statute that is entirely about them. USTR opened the investigations on March 12, made findings on June 2, took more than 1,600 written comments, heard more than 100 witnesses on July 7-9, and differentiated the outcome: Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago and Jordan moved from 12.5 to 10 percent after adopting or committing to prohibitions. And the underlying grievance is not manufactured — the ILO counts 27.6 million people in forced labour, 63 percent of it in the private economy, and the Steelworkers' and Machinists' endorsements show the concern crosses the partisan line.
right.weakestPoint: Two claims doing heavy work do not survive their own sources. Ambassador Greer said the U.S. ban has existed 'for nearly a century' and is 'rigorously' enforced; 19 U.S.C. 1307 does date to 1930, but its consumptive-demand proviso — exempting goods not produced domestically in sufficient quantity — was not struck until Public Law 114-125 on February 24, 2016, so the rigorous-enforcement era is a decade old, not a century. And the remedy overshoots the finding: the tariffs are economy-wide rather than confined to forced-labor goods, they reach economies covering roughly 99.4 percent of U.S. imports, and they took effect on the exact day the Section 122 surcharge hit its statutory 150-day ceiling. That sequencing was not improvised; in February, CFR President and former USTR Michael Froman described the announced plan as using Section 122's 150 days 'to launch and complete processes under other authorities, such as Sections 201, 232, 301, or 338,' with the combination expected to 'substitute for' the struck-down revenue. A policy can be both sincerely aimed at forced labor and designed to reproduce a tariff the Court voided — but the administration cannot claim the first while its own published sequence documents the second.
right.unknowns: Whether USTR's administrative record actually supports the country-by-country findings — which economies lack prohibitions, which fail to enforce, and how much U.S. commerce each failure burdens — cannot be assessed without the record itself, which was not published in the documents read. Whether the rates would in fact fall further if countries tighten their laws is unknowable: Section 301 has no formal adjustment process, and the seven reductions are the only data point. Whether the tariffs will produce measurable reductions in forced labor abroad, as the Southern Shrimp Alliance asserts they already have, is not established by any evidence read.

facts.claim: On July 23-24, 2026 the administration imposed Section 301 tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies — roughly 99.4 percent of U.S. imports — based on their failure to impose or effectively enforce prohibitions on importing goods made with forced labor.
facts.evidence: White House presidential memorandum, signed July 23, 2026 (read directly): authority is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2411); 10 percent on Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom and Trinidad and Tobago; 12.5 percent on the other investigated economies; rates net of MFN for the EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan; finding that 'the acts, policies, and practices of each of these economies are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.' TIME (read directly): the partners 'represent about 99.4% of U.S. imports.'
facts.explanation: The core facts of the action are undisputed and come from the primary document. Two caveats belong here. First, the effective date carries a minor source conflict: Troutman Pepper Locke's analysis says the duties apply to goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. ET on July 24, 2026 with an in-transit grace period to July 28, while Fox Business and Fortune described the tariffs as taking effect as the Section 122 duties expired 'Friday' — July 24, 2026 was a Friday, and the discrepancy in some accounts is noted rather than resolved. Second, '99.4 percent of imports' describes the share attributable to the covered economies, not the share of import value actually taxed: energy, fertilizer, certain foods, USMCA-qualifying Canadian and Mexican goods, pharmaceuticals and articles already under Section 232 are exempt, and no document read quantifies the net coverage.
facts.source: The White House — Actions by the United States in the Investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (60 economies, forced labor)

corroboration.source: USTR — USTR Takes Action in Forced Labor Section 301 Investigations (July 23, 2026)
TIME — Trump's New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries, Explained (July 24, 2026)
Fox Business (right-leaning) — Trump administration unveils new tariffs on 60 trading partners

facts.claim: The new tariffs took effect on the exact day the administration's temporary Section 122 surcharge hit the statutory 150-day maximum that Congress imposed on that authority.
facts.evidence: 19 U.S.C. 2132 (read directly at Cornell LII): authorizes 'a temporary import surcharge, not to exceed 15 percent ad valorem' 'for a period not exceeding 150 days (unless such period is extended by Act of Congress).' Covington & Burling (February 27, 2026 alert, read directly): the 10 percent Section 122 surcharge 'took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026' and expires 'July 24, 2026' at the end of the 150-day period. TIME (read directly): Trump 'responded with temporary tariffs under Section 122 on February 24, which could only last 150 days unless Congress extended them.'
facts.explanation: This is arithmetic against statutory text and it holds exactly: February 24 plus 150 days is July 24, and Congress did not extend the surcharge. The fact is graded on the timing alone, which is checkable; the inference critics draw from it — that the forced-labor finding was engineered to arrive on schedule — is a motive claim addressed separately below. The strongest contrary consideration is that USTR opened the 60 investigations on March 12, only weeks after the Section 122 surcharge began, and that Section 304 gives USTR up to twelve months to determine; completing in four months is fast but not outside the statute, and a deadline-driven schedule is consistent with either a pretext or an administration trying to avoid a gap in a policy it sincerely holds.
facts.source: 19 U.S.C. 2132 — Balance-of-payments authority (Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974), Cornell LII

corroboration.source: Covington & Burling — IEEPA Tariffs Terminated, Replacement Section 122 Tariffs Take Effect (Feb. 27, 2026)
TIME — Trump's New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries, Explained

facts.claim: The Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs — but the ruling did not address Section 301, which is an explicit congressional delegation of tariff authority.
facts.evidence: National Law Review summary of Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (read directly): '6-3 decision issued February 20, 2026'; the Court 'determined that IEEPA does not authorize presidential tariff imposition'; Chief Justice Roberts 'invoked the major questions doctrine, requiring "clear congressional authorization"'; the statute authorizes the President to 'regulate importation' but 'contains no explicit tariff language'; Justices Thomas, Kavanaugh and Alito dissented. 19 U.S.C. 2411(b) (read directly): where a practice 'is unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts United States commerce,' the Trade Representative 'shall take all appropriate and feasible action authorized under subsection (c)' — which includes duties.
facts.explanation: Both halves matter and each side tends to drop one. Critics who say the Court 'already ruled these tariffs illegal' are overstating: the holding turned on IEEPA's silence about tariffs, and Section 301 is a statute whose entire purpose is authorizing trade remedies including duties. Defenders who say the ruling is irrelevant are also overstating: the Court's reasoning was major-questions reasoning about clear authorization for actions of vast economic significance, which the Congressional Research Service expressly flagged as a live problem for a Section 301 action reaching more than 99 percent of U.S. imports. Confidence is high on the holding; the opinion PDF at supremecourt.gov was not fetched, and the vote, date, author and reasoning were confirmed in the National Law Review summary read directly and are consistent across every secondary account encountered.
facts.source: National Law Review — SCOTUS Rules on Tariffs in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump

corroboration.source: Supreme Court of the United States — Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, No. 24-1287 (Feb. 20, 2026) [slip opinion PDF; not fetched directly]
19 U.S.C. 2411 (Section 301), Cornell LII — the express tariff-remedy delegation

facts.claim: Ambassador Greer's statement that the United States 'has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it' overstates the record: the 1930 ban's 'consumptive demand' exception was not repealed until February 24, 2016.
facts.evidence: Greer, via Fox Business (right-leaning, read directly): 'The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same.' 19 U.S.C. 1307 (read directly at Cornell LII): bans goods 'mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part in any foreign country by convict labor or/and forced labor or/and indentured labor under penal sanctions'; the source credits show Pub. L. 114-125 (February 24, 2016) removed the provision exempting goods 'not mined, produced, or manufactured in such quantities in the United States as to meet the consumptive demands of the United States,' and Pub. L. 106-200 (May 18, 2000) added forced or indentured child labor.
facts.explanation: Graded mixed because the first clause is true and the second is not. The prohibition genuinely dates to the Tariff Act of 1930, so 'nearly a century' is accurate as to the statute's existence. But for 86 of those 96 years the consumptive-demand exception exempted precisely the goods the United States did not make enough of domestically — the category most likely to be imported — and the ban was correspondingly little used until the 2016 repeal and the enforcement build-out that followed. 'Rigorously enforces it' describes the last decade, not the century. The overstatement matters because the moral asymmetry between the U.S. and its partners is the rhetorical foundation of the whole action; on the statute's own timeline the United States closed its own loophole ten years ago. CBP's enforcement statistics page returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, so no figure on detained shipments is asserted here.
facts.source: 19 U.S.C. 1307 — Convict-made goods; importation prohibited (Cornell LII, with source credits)

corroboration.source: Fox Business (right-leaning) — Trump administration unveils new tariffs on 60 trading partners (the Greer quote)
Fortune — Trump reimposes tariffs on 60 countries using forced-labor law (same Greer quote)

facts.claim: Section 301's enumerated 'unreasonable' practices include a persistent pattern of conduct that 'permits any form of forced or compulsory labor' — a country's own labor practices — not a failure to prohibit imports of forced-labor goods; but the statutory list is expressly non-exhaustive.
facts.evidence: 19 U.S.C. 2411(d)(3)(B) (read directly at Cornell LII): 'Acts, policies, and practices that are unreasonable include, but are not limited to, any act, policy, or practice… which— … (iii) constitutes a persistent pattern of conduct that— (I) denies workers the right of association, (II) denies workers the right to organize and bargain collectively, (III) permits any form of forced or compulsory labor, (IV) fails to provide a minimum age for the employment of children, or (V) fails to provide standards for minimum wages, hours of work, and occupational safety and health of workers.' CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11460 (July 21, 2026, read via EveryCRSReport): courts may review whether the conduct qualifies as an actionable 'act, policy, or practice,' with 'uncertainty… about whether conduct must rise to a "persistent pattern"' and whether that means duration or obstinacy.
facts.explanation: This is the hinge of the litigation and both readings are defensible from the text. The enumerated clause is about a government permitting forced labor within its own jurisdiction; USTR's theory is one step removed — that failing to block forced-labor goods at the border is itself an unreasonable practice burdening U.S. commerce, on the reasoning stated in its June 2 findings that such failures let firms using forced labor 'produce goods at lower cost and thereby distort market conditions.' Because the list is prefaced 'include, but are not limited to,' the mismatch with clause (iii)(III) is not dispositive, and the general definition of 'unreasonable' as unfair and inequitable is broad. But it does mean the administration is not standing on the clause it most resembles, which is why CRS treats actionability as a genuine question rather than a settled one. Graded supported as a description of the statute and the dispute, not as a prediction of which reading wins.

corroboration.source: CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11460 — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity (July 21, 2026), via EveryCRSReport [congress.gov returned HTTP 403]
USTR — USTR Makes Findings and Proposes Action in 60 Section 301 Investigations (June 2, 2026), stating the theory of harm

facts.claim: USTR conducted a full statutory process — 60 investigations opened March 12, 2026, findings June 2, more than 1,600 written comments and more than 100 witnesses across hearings in April and July — and cut rates from 12.5 to 10 percent for seven economies that adopted or committed to forced-labor import prohibitions.
facts.evidence: USTR release of July 23, 2026 (read directly): 'Investigations initiated March 12, 2026; public hearings held April 28-29, 2026; final determination June 2, 2026; additional hearings July 7-9, 2026 with 100+ witnesses and 1,600+ written comments reviewed.' IELP blog (Simon Lester, read directly): Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago and Jordan 'already received reduced rates (12.5% to 10%)' after improving their laws, with the White House saying the reductions aim 'to further encourage these economies to effectively enforce such prohibitions.'
facts.explanation: The procedural record is real and is the administration's best answer to the pretext charge: a fabricated rationale does not usually generate two rounds of hearings, 1,600 comments and differentiated country outcomes. Confidence is medium rather than high for a specific reason: the process facts come from the agency that ran the process and from a blog summarizing the White House memorandum, and the underlying administrative record — the country-by-country findings supporting each determination — has not been published in anything read here, which is precisely the gap the Court of International Trade complaint targets. The strongest contrary point is that a real process can still produce a remedy untethered from its findings; procedural regularity and pretext are not mutually exclusive.
facts.source: USTR — USTR Takes Action in Forced Labor Section 301 Investigations (July 23, 2026)

corroboration.source: IELP Blog (Simon Lester) — listing the seven economies moved from 12.5 to 10 percent and quoting the White House rationale
USTR — June 2, 2026 findings release (initiation date, determination, proposed rates)

facts.claim: The tariffs apply economy-wide rather than only to goods made with forced labor, and the Congressional Research Service flagged before the action that this scope invites major-questions and administrative-record challenges.
facts.evidence: Troutman Pepper Locke (read directly): the tariffs apply 'economy-wide rather than only to forced-labor goods,' making the remedy 'broader in geographic and sectoral scope than traditional Section 301 investigations,' and the memorandum includes a severability clause so that if a court invalidates the tariff 'applicable to any one trading partner, that ruling does not affect the tariffs applicable to any other trading partner.' CRS LSB11460 (July 21, 2026, read directly via EveryCRSReport): if USTR imposes tariffs on 60 countries representing 'more than 99% of U.S. imports,' challengers may argue this is an 'unheralded' and 'transformational' use of the statute requiring 'clear congressional authorization'; courts could also scrutinize whether USTR adequately supported that the failures 'burden' U.S. commerce and that the rates are proportionate; Section 301 actions face APA 'arbitrary and capricious' review in the Court of International Trade rather than the deference given presidential tariff actions.
facts.explanation: Both elements are documented and neither is a partisan characterization: the scope point comes from a trade law firm's client alert describing the memorandum, and the vulnerability analysis comes from Congress's own nonpartisan research service three days before the action. The severability clause is itself evidence that the administration anticipated country-specific losses. The honest counterweight is that CRS identifies questions, not answers — it does not predict that the tariffs fall, and Section 301(c) does give USTR broad remedial discretion, including duties 'unconnected to specific products involved in the investigated conduct' as Troutman notes. So the scope is unusual and legally exposed, not self-evidently unlawful.
facts.source: CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11460 — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity (July 21, 2026), via EveryCRSReport

corroboration.source: Troutman Pepper Locke — Forced Labor, Meet Section 301: New Tariffs Target 60 of America's Biggest Trading Partners
The White House — the memorandum itself (economy-wide application and country lists)

facts.claim: Two small importers, represented by the conservative-libertarian Liberty Justice Center, sued in the U.S. Court of International Trade on July 24, 2026, alleging the forced-labor rationale is a pretext for recreating the tariffs the Supreme Court struck down.
facts.evidence: Liberty Justice Center press release (read directly): filed July 24, 2026 in the U.S. Court of International Trade for plaintiffs Burlap & Barrel, Inc. and Collective Horology; the complaint alleges USTR failed to establish, for each economy, 'the specific act being challenged, how it burdens U.S. commerce, why the tariff rate is appropriate, and how tariffs will eliminate the practice.' CEO Sara Albrecht: 'Forced labor is morally indefensible, but an important objective does not give the government permission to ignore the law.' Senior Counsel Jeffrey Schwab: 'Section 301 is a targeted, country-specific and practice-specific remedial authority. It is not a freestanding authorization to tax substantially all imports from substantially all countries.'
facts.explanation: This is graded 'both' deliberately: the legal attack on a Republican president's tariffs is being led by a conservative-libertarian public-interest firm, not by a progressive one, and the plaintiffs' own statement concedes the moral seriousness of forced labor while contesting the remedy. That cross-cutting alignment is the strongest available corroboration that the pretext objection is not merely partisan. Confidence is high on the filing, plaintiffs, court and quotes, all read in the firm's own release; InsideTrade's independent report is paywalled and only its lede — describing 'a pair of small importers' alleging 'pretext' — was visible. What remains unknown is the merits: a complaint is an allegation, no court had ruled as of July 24, and the memorandum's severability clause is designed to limit the damage from any single adverse ruling.
facts.source: Liberty Justice Center — Liberty Justice Center Challenges Unlawful Section 301 Tariffs as Administration Replaces Expiring Section 122 Tariffs

corroboration.source: InsideTrade — Importers sue over 301 tariffs, claiming forced labor was used as a pretext [paywalled; lede only]
IELP Blog (Simon Lester) — noting the suit's claim that 'the purported rationale of addressing forced labor is simply a pretext for tariffs'

facts.claim: Forced labor is a real and large global problem: the ILO estimates 27.6 million people are in forced labour, with 63 percent of it in the private economy.
facts.evidence: International Labour Organization forced labour topic page (read directly): '27.6 million of men, women and children are in forced labour' (2022 Global Estimates); '63% of forced labour happens in the private economy,' generating illegal profits estimated at '236 billion US$ every year' (2024 analysis).
facts.explanation: The premise underneath the administration's action is well founded and should be credited even by those who think the remedy unlawful — this is not an invented problem. Confidence is medium rather than high for provenance reasons the protocol requires flagging: the 27.6 million figure is a modeled global estimate produced by the ILO with Walk Free and IOM, not a count, it dates to 2022, and the ILO is an interested institution in the sense that the estimate underwrites its own mandate. It is nonetheless the standard reference figure used across the political spectrum. What the figure does not establish is the step USTR needs: how much of that forced labour enters U.S. commerce through the 60 economies' import channels, or how much a 10-12.5 percent economy-wide tariff would reduce it. No source read quantifies either.
facts.source: International Labour Organization — Forced labour, modern slavery and trafficking in persons

corroboration.source: USTR — American Steelworkers, Manufacturers, and Farmers Praise President Trump's Tariff Action to Combat Forced Labor (union and industry endorsements of the premise)

powerLens.thesis: The power test here is unusually clean because the same statute has been fired in both directions within twenty-six months. In May 2024 a Democratic administration used Section 301, after a USTR 'statutory four-year review,' to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles from 25 to 100 percent, solar cells from 25 to 50 percent, and semiconductors toward 50 percent, covering $18 billion of imports — and Democrats called it protecting American workers while free-market conservatives called it politics in an election year. In July 2026 a Republican administration uses the same statute, after the same kind of USTR process, and Democrats call it a lawless tariff tantrum while conservatives who spent the Biden years insisting that Congress holds the taxing power are split between defending it and suing to stop it. The second mirror is doctrinal: the major questions doctrine was built by the conservative legal movement to strike executive actions of vast economic significance lacking clear congressional authorization, and in February 2026 Chief Justice Roberts turned it on Trump's own tariffs — so the administration now argues for expansive readings of delegated power while the conservative-libertarian Liberty Justice Center presses the doctrine its own coalition made, and progressives who called the doctrine a judicial power grab find it suddenly congenial. Each tribe's view of how much tariff power Congress delegated tracks who is currently wielding it. The needle, though, rests on the present record: what the statute says, when the Section 122 clock ran out, what the remedy actually taxes, and whether the government's own claims survive their own sources.

precedent.case: The Biden administration's May 14, 2024 Section 301 tariff increases on China — set against the February 20, 2026 major-questions ruling that struck Trump's IEEPA tariffs.
precedent.what: On May 14, 2024, following what the White House called 'an in-depth review by the United States Trade Representative' under Section 301, the Biden administration raised the tariff on Chinese electric vehicles 'from 25% to 100% in 2024,' solar cells 'from 25% to 50% in 2024,' steel and aluminum 'from 0-7.5% to 25% in 2024,' and semiconductors 'from 25% to 50% by 2025,' covering '$18 billion of imports from China' — unilateral executive tariff-setting on a scale no Congress voted on, defended as protecting American workers from unfair practices. Twenty-one months later, on February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court held 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, with the Chief Justice applying the major questions doctrine's demand for 'clear congressional authorization' — the doctrine conservatives had built against Biden-era executive action.
precedent.mirror: Map either precedent onto July 24, 2026 and the roles swap. The party whose president is setting the tariffs discovers that Section 301 is a broad, flexible delegation for confronting unfair foreign practices; the party out of power discovers that the Constitution gives Congress the taxing power and that USTR reviews are a fig leaf. The legal doctrine follows the same rule: major questions was a conservative instrument against progressive agencies until it became the instrument that voided a Republican president's signature economic policy, at which point conservatives litigating trade cases embraced it and the administration's defenders discovered its limits. Neither the 'Congress holds the tariff power' principle nor the 'USTR review is real process' principle has survived a change in whose ox is gored.
precedent.source: Biden White House archive — FACT SHEET: President Biden Takes Action to Protect American Workers and Businesses from China's Unfair Trade Practices (May 14, 2024)

corroboration.source: National Law Review — summary of Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (major questions doctrine, 'clear congressional authorization')
CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11460 — applying the major questions framing to the Section 301 forced-labor action

flips.then: On May 14, 2024, a Democratic White House announced that under Section 301, following a USTR review, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles would rise 'from 25% to 100% in 2024,' solar cells 'from 25% to 50%,' and steel and aluminum 'from 0-7.5% to 25%,' across '$18 billion of imports from China' — executive tariff-setting by agency determination, without a congressional vote, defended as protecting American workers from unfair trade practices. Congressional Democrats broadly supported it, and the same coalition had passed forced-labor trade enforcement legislation with overwhelming bipartisan majorities.
flips.now: In July 2026 the ranking Democrat on Ways and Means, Rep. Richard Neal, dismisses a Section 301 action on forced labor with 'Today's forced labor justification is too convenient to be taken seriously,' and the Senate Finance ranking member's response is titled a statement on the president's 'latest tariff tantrum.' The objection that unilateral USTR tariff-setting is illegitimate arrives from the party that used the identical authority to quadruple a tariff rate two years earlier — the difference being who signs the determination.
flips.source: Biden White House archive — FACT SHEET on the May 14, 2024 Section 301 increases (the 'then')

flips.then: The conservative legal movement spent the Biden years building the major questions doctrine — the rule that an agency claiming power of vast economic and political significance must point to 'clear congressional authorization' — and conservative public-interest firms deployed it against executive action they considered untethered from statute. Republicans in Congress made 'the Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to lay duties' a standard line against executive trade and regulatory unilateralism.
flips.now: In 2026 that doctrine, applied by Chief Justice Roberts in Learning Resources, voided the administration's own tariffs — and the administration responded by moving the same global tariff to Section 122, then to Section 232, then to Section 301, arguing for the broadest available reading of each delegation. The conservative-libertarian Liberty Justice Center is now the one telling a Republican administration that 'Section 301 is a targeted, country-specific and practice-specific remedial authority… not a freestanding authorization to tax substantially all imports from substantially all countries.' The right is flipping against itself in real time, which is at least more honest than flipping in unison.
flips.source: Liberty Justice Center — press release on its July 24, 2026 Court of International Trade complaint (a conservative-libertarian firm suing a Republican administration)

powerLens.longRun: Strip out who occupies the White House and the through-line is that Congress delegated its tariff power decades ago and has never wanted it back badly enough to vote. Section 122 (1974), Section 232 (1962), Section 301 (1974) and Section 338 (1930) are a menu, and every modern president has ordered from it — Obama and Biden under 301 against China, Trump under 232, IEEPA, 122 and now 301 against nearly everyone. The Supreme Court's February ruling narrowed the menu by one item without touching the others, and within five months the same policy had migrated to a statute that survived. The prediction when power changes hands is unusually easy: a future Democratic administration will find Section 301 an excellent vehicle for climate-, labor- or supply-chain-conditioned tariffs, will describe the process as rigorous and the authority as clear, and today's defenders of executive trade power will rediscover that the Constitution vests taxation in Congress. The durable question — whether Congress will ever attach a hard rate ceiling, a sunset, or a legislative-approval requirement to the delegations it wrote in 1930, 1962 and 1974 — remains unanswered, and the Section 122 episode shows why: the one delegation Congress did cap, at 15 percent and 150 days, worked exactly as designed and was simply replaced by an uncapped one.
powerLens.appliedToScore: The power test docks reasoning honesty on both sides and gives neither a consistency bonus. Democrats objecting to unilateral Section 301 tariff-setting cannot invoke a principle their own administration spent 2024 disregarding, and 'the justification is too convenient to be taken seriously' is an argument about motive that the same politicians would have rejected if aimed at the 100-percent EV tariff. The administration, for its part, cannot invoke the sanctity of statutory text while stretching a clause about countries that 'permit' forced labor to cover countries that fail to police imports, nor claim surprise at major-questions scrutiny from a doctrine its own coalition built. But the needle rests on present-tense checkable facts, not consistency: does the Section 122 clock expire the day the new tariffs begin (yes, by statute and arithmetic); does the remedy reach only forced-labor goods (no, it is economy-wide); did USTR run a real statutory process (yes, with 1,600-plus comments and two rounds of hearings); is the U.S. ban rigorously enforced across 'nearly a century' (no, the consumptive-demand exception survived until 2016); is forced labor a real problem (yes, 27.6 million by the standard estimate); did the Supreme Court already resolve this (no). The critics' checkable claims land more often than the administration's, which is why the needle leans left — modestly, because the legal question is open and the administration's process and premise are real.
powerLens.unknowns: The power test measures consistency of principle, not who is right today. That both parties have used Section 301 unilaterally does not make the uses equivalent in scale: Biden's May 2024 action covered $18 billion of imports from one country, while this one reaches economies accounting for roughly 99.4 percent of all U.S. imports. Whether Democrats would accept an identical action from their own president, and whether the conservative legal movement would have sued a Democratic administration on the same theory with the same speed, cannot be known from the present record.

pattern.thesis: The forced-labor tariff is not a stand-alone trade action; it is the fourth statute in five months through which the administration has reached substantially the same global tariff after the Supreme Court removed the first, and judging it in isolation is exactly the frame that makes it look like a human-rights measure rather than a revenue and leverage program. The sequence is public and documented: IEEPA tariffs struck down February 20, 2026; a 10 percent Section 122 balance-of-payments surcharge in place four days later, on the one authority Congress capped at 15 percent and 150 days; Section 232 national-security tariffs expanded through the spring, including 100 percent duties on patented pharmaceuticals from most countries in April, waivable for drugmakers who sign pricing agreements; and on July 24, the day the Section 122 cap expired, a Section 301 forced-labor tariff on 60 economies. In February, CFR President and former U.S. Trade Representative Michael Froman described this exact path as the announced strategy. Each step has a real statutory hook and a defensible-sounding rationale in isolation; the pattern is one administration cycling through every delegation Congress ever wrote until it finds one a court has not yet closed, with the tariff level held roughly constant throughout.

campaigns.where: Section 122 — the 150-day bridge, February 24 to July 24, 2026
campaigns.what: Four days after the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, a 10 percent global surcharge took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026 under Section 122's balance-of-payments authority — the one tariff delegation Congress explicitly capped, at 15 percent ad valorem and 150 days 'unless such period is extended by Act of Congress.' Congress did not extend it, and it expired on July 24, 2026, the day the Section 301 tariffs took effect.

A national-security statute used as leverage in a domestic drug-pricing negotiation.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is not whether any single tariff is defensible — several have real statutory hooks and at least one has genuine bipartisan support — but whether a policy that keeps its rate roughly constant while cycling through four different legal justifications in five months is best understood by its stated rationale or by its constant. The 'one-off' tell to watch: commentary that debates whether forced labor is a serious problem (it is) without noting that the tariff falls on all goods rather than forced-labor goods, arrived the day a statutory clock expired, and follows a path an ex-USTR sketched publicly in February — or, from the other direction, commentary that treats the whole thing as transparently fake and thereby never has to engage the ILO's 27.6 million, the 1,600 comments, the two rounds of hearings, or the seven countries whose rates fell when their laws improved. The facts that do not move: the Section 122 cap expired July 24, the new tariffs are economy-wide, USTR ran a real process, and no court had ruled either way as of that date.
pattern.unknowns: The pattern is context that reframes the stakes, not a thumb on the needle, which rests on the day's checkable facts. A sequence of statute substitutions is consistent with an administration cynically laundering a revenue policy through whatever authority survives judicial review, and also with an administration that believes in tariffs, lost one legal vehicle, and used the others Congress gave it — the record does not distinguish motive, and the seven conduct-based rate reductions are real evidence against the purely cynical reading. Whether the Court of International Trade treats the pattern as evidence of pretext or as irrelevant to whether the statute's conditions were met is the central open question.

notAdjudicable: Whether tariffs are an appropriate instrument for enforcing labor and human-rights standards abroad — as against sanctions, import bans on specific goods, procurement rules, or diplomacy — is a values and strategy question that no evidence about forced-labor prevalence can settle by itself.

Whether the cost to American consumers and importers is worth the leverage gained over trading partners is a tradeoff between domestic purchasing power and foreign labor conditions, and people who agree on every number will still disagree about the exchange rate between them.

Whether Congress should reclaim the tariff power it delegated in 1930, 1962 and 1974 — by capping rates, adding sunsets, or requiring an up-or-down vote — is a constitutional-design judgment, not a factual dispute; both parties have benefited from the delegation and neither has moved to repeal it.

Whether a government action can be legitimate when its stated purpose is sincere but not its only purpose is a question about political morality that courts answer narrowly and citizens answer differently; 'mixed motives' is a description, not a verdict.

Whether it is fair to tax an entire economy for its government's failure to police goods produced by coercion somewhere else in the supply chain — spreading the cost across innocent producers to reach a wrong they did not commit — is a question of collective responsibility that no trade statistic resolves.
biasWatch: The bias most clouding this issue is motive-reading in both directions: the assumption that a policy's real purpose is knowable from whether you like the person announcing it. If you distrust the president, the forced-labor rationale is transparently fake and there is nothing further to examine; if you trust him, the timing is a coincidence and the critics are simply pro-China. Both shortcuts spare you the only work that matters, which is comparing what the statute authorizes to what the remedy actually does. The tell to watch, in commentary and in yourself: does the writer ever distinguish between the finding and the remedy — between 'these countries fail to block forced-labor imports' and 'therefore tax all their goods at 10 to 12.5 percent' — and does the writer acknowledge the facts that cut against them? A critic who never mentions the 1,600 comments, the two rounds of hearings, or the seven countries whose rates fell when their laws improved is running on motive. A defender who never mentions that the tariffs took effect the day the Section 122 clock expired, that they fall on all goods rather than forced-labor goods, or that the U.S. ban Greer called rigorously enforced 'for nearly a century' had a consumptive-demand loophole until 2016, is doing the same. Then apply the swap test, which this issue fails cleanly in both directions: if you cheered a Democratic USTR raising Chinese EV tariffs from 25 to 100 percent by administrative determination in May 2024, you owe an explanation for calling the identical mechanism lawless now; if you spent the Biden years insisting that agencies claiming vast economic power need clear congressional authorization, you owe one for objecting when a conservative-libertarian law firm says exactly that to this administration. And keep what the swap test cannot erase: whichever party had done it, 27.6 million people would still be in forced labour, the Section 122 cap would still have expired on July 24, and no court had yet said which reading of Section 301 wins.
